transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Brazil's incumbent President Luis Ignacio Lula da Silva has won re-election.
He defeated his remaining rival yesterday in the last round of Brazil's national elections.
NPR's Kerry Kahn says Lula had come in second place in the initial round of voting, and
he had to gather more support.
He needed to get out the vote. Some 33 million Brazilians had sat out that first round, and
polls just predicted he was done.
He would need to pick up a large majority of fresh votes in the second round to win,
and that's exactly what he did. Brazilians went to the polls.
He outperformed Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the former far-right president, by more than
four million votes.
I think Lula, who turns 81 tomorrow, was even shocked by the turnaround himself.
NPR's Kerry Kahn reporting.
President Trump will campaign in Mississippi today for Republican candidates.
He did that over the weekend in Michigan and Ohio.
So did former President Barack Obama, who stumped for Democratic candidates.
The midterms are just over a week away, and millions of people have already voted.
NPR's Tamara Keith checks in on the mid-decade redistricting effort that was supposed to
help Republicans.
President Trump and his political team pressured Republican-led states to redraw congressional
district lines, and they were able to shift 15 districts nationwide to favor the party's
candidates.
But now, only a third of those districts look like a sure thing for Republicans.
Nathan Gonzalez is editor of Inside Elections.
Redistricting was supposed to be a firewall for Republicans in this midterm election, and
it has just not turned out that way.
Instead, the redrawn districts include some of the most competitive and expensive House
races in the country.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Three judges from the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals held an unusual hearing yesterday.
It was over the Justice Department's lawsuit against California over its voter rolls.
As NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports, the DOJ is demanding that California officials put
aside ballots from 20,000 registered voters.
The DOJ says the registered voters in question are likely non-citizens, and is arguing that
California election officials must be stopped from processing their ballots.
Lawyers for the state in Los Angeles County have argued that the DOJ's list is unreliable
in doing what the federal government demands would be unlawful and logistically infeasible
at this point.
A federal judge set a hearing in the case for this Tuesday, but before that could happen,
the DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit, arguing the lower court wasn't moving fast enough.
In the Sunday hearing, two of the three judges on the panel had hard questions for the DOJ
attorney, both about the department's demands and whether the appeals court can even weigh
in at this stage.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
There are flood warnings still posted for the Four Corners area in the desert southwest.
That's Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah.
The National Weather Service says there has been catastrophic flooding along the San Juan
River.
Officials in New Mexico have asked some local residents to stay out of their homes for safety.
A startup company in Texas is working to produce a new generation of military and police dogs
through genetic engineering.
But as NPR's Windsor Johnston reports, scientists say the technology may be years away from
delivering on that promise.
The startup Warhound has raised $200 million to develop cloned and genetically engineered
dogs with improved health and working abilities.
Cornell University animal geneticist Heather Houson says the technology exists, but scientists
still don't know which genes control traits like endurance and behavior.
I do appreciate the high risk, high reward, really reaching for the stars type of projects,
which I think this is doing.
One of my big things of being cautious, this isn't going to happen overnight.
Warhound's website says it's certified by the American Humane Society.
But in a statement to NPR, the organization says its partnership with the company is still
evolving.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
A historic ocean liner is closer to becoming the world's biggest artificial reef.
Animal officials in Florida are going to submerge the S.S. United States off the Gulf Coast
in November.
They want to make it a destination for divers.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Brazil's President Lula da Silva wins re-election, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro in the runoff
Trump to campaign in Mississippi for Republican candidates ahead of midterms
Mid-decade redistricting effort meant to help Republicans falls short, per Inside Elections editor
Ninth Circuit hears DOJ appeal in lawsuit over California voter rolls and 20,000 ballots
Flood warnings remain in Four Corners region after catastrophic San Juan River flooding
Texas startup Warhound seeks genetically engineered military and police dogs; scientists skeptical
S.S. United States to be sunk off Florida Gulf Coast as artificial reef in November
